opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that we only partially know. Let me tell you how I like to think about it.

My starting point is that the structure of the data matters more than the details of the architecture. Real data like images or text is compositional: small features combine into larger ones, which combine into larger ones still. If that hierarchy is really there, then any network that learns the task efficiently has to discover it in some form. That's the intuition behind the toy models my group has worked on, like the random hierarchy model. In those models, the latent variables at each level of the hierarchy aren't arbitrary choices the network makes. They're dictated by the generative process. So if two architectures both succeed at learning the task with a reasonable number of examples, they should end up representing something close to the same latent variables.

How do they find those variables? Through correlations. Parts of the input that are synonymous, meaning they play the same role at a higher level, have the same correlations with the label or with the surrounding context. A network can detect those correlations once it has seen enough data. That's what lets it group synonyms together and build invariant representations, level by level. This mechanism belongs to the data, not to the particular network. So I'd expect convergence in what is represented.

That said, I want to add some nuance. Convergence of the abstractions doesn't mean the networks learn equally efficiently. Architecture changes the sample complexity a lot. A convolutional network whose locality and weight sharing match the structure of the data can build the hierarchy with far fewer examples than a fully connected network. A fully connected network may not get there at all in a practical regime. Transformers sit somewhere in between: they're flexible enough to discover the structure, but they pay a price in data compared with an architecture where the right prior is built in. So I'd say there's convergence at the level of what's eventually learned, and divergence in how fast and whether it's learned at all.

The second nuance is that real data isn't a clean tree. The hierarchy is approximate, there are many ways to describe the same structure, and the network's representation is distributed. So when people measure representational similarity across models, they find quite a lot of alignment, especially at intermediate and deeper layers. But it's not identity, and it shouldn't be. Some aspects of the representation are forced by the data. Others are just a matter of parametrization.

So my short answer is: to the extent the data has genuine hierarchical, compositional structure, successful architectures should converge on similar abstractions, because those abstractions are essentially the latent variables of the data. Architecture mostly determines the cost of getting there. Disentangling those two effects, what's forced by the data versus what's a choice of the model, is to me one of the most interesting open questions in the theory of deep learning.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I find really interesting, because I think the honest answer is: more than you'd naively expect, but for reasons that have more to do with the data than with the architectures.

Let me explain what I mean. The view we've been developing in my group is that the reason deep learning works on things like images or language is that the data itself has a hierarchical, compositional structure. A cat is made of a head and a body, the head is made of ears and eyes, and so on, down to edges and textures. And crucially, there's a lot of invariance at each level: an ear can look many different ways, and the cat is still a cat. So if you want to learn this kind of task with a reasonable amount of data, you essentially have no choice but to discover this hierarchy and to become insensitive to the irrelevant variations at each level. We've been able to show this quite precisely in simplified generative models, these random hierarchy models, where you can compute how many samples a network needs and show that learning happens exactly when the network manages to build representations that collapse synonyms, meaning different low-level features that play the same role at the next level up.

Now, the key point for your question is that this structure is a property of the task, not of the model. So any architecture that succeeds with a sample complexity close to optimal must, in some sense, have found that same hierarchy. The abstractions are forced on you by the data. That's why I'm not surprised when people find that a convolutional network and a transformer trained on ImageNet end up with representations that are highly aligned, or that you can stitch layers from one network into another and it more or less works. They're both solving the same problem, and the problem has essentially one efficient solution at the level of what should be grouped together.

But I want to be careful, because "the same abstractions" can mean several things, and the convergence is much stronger at some levels than at others. What is really constrained is the partition of the input space, which inputs are treated as equivalent at a given level of the hierarchy. What is not constrained is how that is encoded, how it is distributed across neurons, at which depth it appears, in what coordinate system. A convolutional network has the hierarchy built in spatially, so you'll find it in a very localized way, layer by layer. A transformer has to construct locality itself through attention, and it may represent the same abstraction in a much more spread-out fashion. So if you look at a single neuron, the two look nothing alike. If you look at similarity structure, at which things are close to which, they look very much alike.

There's another important caveat, which is that networks only converge on these abstractions once they are in the regime where they have enough data to learn them. Below the right number of samples, they don't learn the hierarchy at all, they learn something else, some superficial correlation, and in that regime different architectures can diverge quite a lot, because they're each falling back on their own inductive bias. The convergence is a statement about the solution, not about the path to it. And I think a lot of apparent disagreement in the literature comes from comparing networks in different regimes without realizing it.

The last thing I'd say is that there's a bit of selection going on. We are comparing architectures that work. The architectures that work are the ones whose inductive biases let them exploit hierarchy and locality efficiently. A fully connected network on images is also "trained on the same data," and it does not find the same abstractions, or it finds them so inefficiently that in practice it doesn't. So in some sense the convergence we observe is partly because we've already filtered for architectures that are compatible with the structure of the data.

So, to sum up: yes, I expect strong convergence, and I think there's a principled reason for it, which is that hierarchical data admits essentially a unique efficient decomposition and any good learner has to find it. But the convergence is at the level of what gets grouped together, not at the level of how it's physically represented, and only once you're past the point where the network has enough data to actually learn the structure.

astra-6.text:
I think the answer depends on what you mean by the same abstraction. Two networks can make very similar predictions without organizing their internal representations in the same way. So agreement at the level of the output is a weaker statement than agreement about the hierarchy of features.

There are really two things competing here. The data have structure, and if some aspect of that structure is particularly useful for the task, you might expect different networks to discover it. But the architecture and the learning dynamics also introduce a bias: they make certain features easier to learn than others. So I would expect some convergence, but not necessarily a unique hierarchy that every successful network must recover.

And comparing representations is itself subtle. You don't want to ask whether individual neurons are identical, because you can change coordinates and still represent essentially the same information. The more interesting question is whether the networks retain the same distinctions and become insensitive to the same variations. I think that is a more meaningful sense in which they could learn the same abstractions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the answer depends on what we mean by the same abstraction. Two networks can represent information in very different coordinates, so you should not expect individual neurons to correspond. The more interesting question is whether they become sensitive to the same features and invariant to the same transformations.

If the data contain a strong hierarchical structure, and that structure is useful for the task, then I would expect some convergence. Different architectures have an incentive to discover those regularities. But the data and the task do not uniquely determine the representation. There may be several ways to solve the problem, and the architecture and the training dynamics will favor some over others.

So I would distinguish agreement in predictions from agreement in the underlying computation. Two networks can perform equally well on the data we give them and behave differently when we change the distribution. That is where you can start to test whether they have really learned the same abstractions. I would expect partial convergence, but I would be cautious about assuming a universal hierarchy.
